pages.c09-p01: Describe the main features of an integrated development environment (IDE), including the editor, preferences, compiler and debugging tools
pages.c09-p02: Explain the process of translation and the differences between assemblers, compilers and interpreters
pages.c09-p03: Explain the terms syntax, data type and variable, and use the data types integer, real, character, string and Boolean appropriately
pages.c09-p04: Explain the use of variables and constants, and declare, initialise and assign them in a high-level language
pages.c09-p05: Use arithmetic, relational and Boolean (logical) operators, including integer division and modulus, and evaluate conditions
pages.c09-p06: Write programs that take input from the user, convert it to a suitable type and produce formatted output
pages.c09-p07: Describe the fundamental programming concepts of sequence, selection and iteration
pages.c09-p08: Use if, if…else, else if, nested if and switch statements for selection, with conditions built from relational and Boolean operators
pages.c09-p09: Describe count-controlled iteration and use for loops, including loops that count up, down and in steps
pages.c09-p10: Describe condition-controlled iteration and use while (pre-condition) and do…while (post-condition) loops, including sentinel values
pages.c09-p11: Use nested loops and nested selection, and trace programs that combine all three constructs
pages.c09-p12: Explain what is meant by a subroutine and describe the difference between a procedure and a function
pages.c09-p13: Write and call procedures and functions in a high-level language, using parameters, arguments and return values
pages.c09-p14: Explain passing parameters by value and by reference, and predict the effect of each
pages.c09-p15: Explain the scope of local and global variables and the advantages of using local variables
pages.c09-p16: Explain the benefits of modular programming and decomposing a problem into subroutines
pages.c09-p17: Describe the purpose of data structures and distinguish between static and dynamic structures
pages.c09-p18: Use one-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, including traversing them with loops
pages.c09-p19: Use lists as dynamic data structures and justify the choice of a list or an array
pages.c09-p20: Describe and use records to group related fields of different data types
pages.c09-p21: Write to, append to and read from text files, splitting delimited lines into fields
pages.c09-p22: Explain why files are needed for persistent storage and how file errors can be avoided
pages.c09-p23: Describe and use validation checks, and distinguish validation from verification
pages.c09-p24: Use exception handling to deal with run-time errors
pages.c09-p25: Explain the differences between syntax, semantic, run-time and logic errors
pages.c09-p26: Select valid, extreme, invalid and null test data and use a test plan to find errors
pages.c09-p27: Use the debugging tools of an integrated development environment (IDE), such as breakpoints, stepping and watches, to locate errors (IDE features are introduced in AP19)
pages.c09-p28: Explain how the choice of translator (compiler or interpreter, covered in AP19) affects when syntax, semantic and run-time errors are detected

q.q: Which IDE facility would most directly help a team make their combined code look consistent?
o: Preferences that set an agreed layout style
Syntax checking that underlines invalid code
An error list with line numbers
q.why: Preferences let the whole team apply one layout convention, and the IDE can reformat existing code to match.

q.q: How does syntax highlighting help a programmer?
o: Keywords, strings and comments are coloured, so structure is easier to read
Invalid code is underlined with a wavy line before the program is built
Keywords and variable names are suggested after typing a few letters
Blocks that are not being worked on are collapsed to save space
q.why: Highlighting colours different parts of the code, so an unclosed string stands out. The others describe syntax checking, code completion and code folding.

q.q: Which statement about an IDE is correct?
o: Its syntax checker finds every logic error in the code as it is being typed
Its compiler finds all errors, so a program that builds will give correct results
Its syntax checker and compiler catch syntax errors, but logic errors need testing
Its debugging tools fix run-time errors automatically once they are located
q.why: An IDE does not find all errors: logic errors are only found by testing and debugging.

q.q: Which translator produces a one-to-one mapping from instructions to machine code?
q.why: Each assembly mnemonic, such as LDA, corresponds to exactly one machine code instruction.

q.q: A developer wants to sell a game without customers being able to see the source code. Which translator suits this best?
o: An interpreter, because it gives immediate feedback
An assembler, because it is a high-level language
An interpreter, because it produces object code
A compiler, because it produces an executable
q.why: A compiler creates an executable that can be distributed without the source code.

q.q: Why can an interpreted program leave a file half-updated after an error?
o: Statements before the faulty line have already run when the error is found
Interpreters translate the whole program first, then run it all at once
Interpreters delete any file that is open when the program crashes
Interpreters cannot close files, so the last changes are never saved
q.why: An interpreter only finds an error when it reaches that line, after earlier statements have run.

q.q: Why does an interpreted program usually run more slowly than a compiled one?
o: The interpreter produces object code that must be optimised before it runs
The interpreter lists every error together before any statement can run
The interpreter translates into assembly language rather than machine code
Each statement is translated again every time it runs, even inside loops
q.why: An interpreter produces no object code, so translation is repeated on each run and on every pass of a loop.

q.q: Which data type is most suitable for storing a mobile phone number such as 07712 345678?
q.why: It begins with 0, may contain spaces and is never used in arithmetic, so it must be text; an integer would lose the leading zero.

q.q: Which statement is valid C#?
q.why: A char needs single quotes, a bool literal has no quotes, and 15.5 cannot be stored in an int.

q.q: Why do C# programmers prefer decimal to double for money?
o: decimal uses less memory than double, so totals are calculated more quickly
double cannot store any value with a fractional part, such as pounds and pence
decimal stores values such as 0.10 exactly; double can introduce tiny rounding errors
decimal rounds every value to two places automatically when it is stored
q.why: double is a binary type and can introduce tiny rounding errors; decimal stores values like 0.10 exactly.

q.q: Which is a valid C# identifier?
q.why: Identifiers may start with an underscore; they cannot start with a digit, contain spaces or be reserved words.

q.q: After int n = 5; n *= n - 2; what is the value of n?
q.why: The right-hand side is evaluated first: n - 2 = 3, then n = 5 × 3 = 15.

q.q: Which is the main reason for declaring VAT_RATE as a constant?
o: It can be changed by the user at run time whenever the VAT rate changes
It cannot be changed accidentally while running and is updated in one place
It makes the program run faster because constants use no memory at all
It can be given a new value in any subroutine without causing an error
q.why: A constant is protected from change at run time (the compiler rejects assignment) and has a single point of maintenance.

q.q: What does 47 % 8 evaluate to in C#?
q.why: 47 = 5 × 8 + 7, so the remainder is 7. 5 is the result of 47 / 8 (integer division).

q.q: With int a = 7, b = 2; what is a / b?
q.why: Both operands are integers, so C# performs integer division and discards the remainder.

q.q: Which condition is true only when age is from 13 to 19 inclusive?
q.why: Both bounds must hold, so use AND with inclusive operators. Using || is true for every number.

q.q: With int total = 7, count = 2; which expression gives 3.5?
q.why: Casting one operand before dividing forces real division. (double)(total / count) casts after integer division has already given 3.

q.q: What type of value does Console.ReadLine() return?
q.why: It always returns text, even if the user typed digits; conversion is a separate step.

q.q: What is output by Console.WriteLine($"{7.0 / 3:F2}");?
q.why: 7.0 / 3 = 2.333…, which F2 displays to two decimal places.

q.q: What happens if int.Parse is given the text "12a"?
o: A FormatException is thrown at run time
The compiler reports a syntax error
q.why: The text is not a valid integer, so a run-time exception occurs.

q.q: What is output by Console.WriteLine("Total: " + 5 + 3);?
q.why: Once a string is on the left, + joins text, so 5 then 3 are appended. Brackets (5 + 3) would give 8.

q.q: Which construct is used when a program must apply a discount only to orders over £50?
q.why: A condition decides whether the discount statement runs.

q.q: A program reads exactly 30 pupils' marks. Which construct is most appropriate?
q.why: The number of repetitions (30) is known in advance.

q.q: Why does the order of statements in a sequence matter?
o: The compiler always reorders statements, so the order written has no effect on the output
Only the first statement in a sequence runs; the rest are skipped unless a loop is used
Statements in a sequence run at the same time, so their order only affects the speed
Later statements depend on results of earlier ones, so changing the order can change the output
q.why: For example, a total must be calculated after the values are input and before it is output.

q.q: In the chain if (points >= 90) Gold; else if (points >= 75) Silver; else if (points >= 50) Bronze; else Participation, what is the award for 75?
q.why: 75 >= 90 is false, 75 >= 75 is true, so Silver is assigned and the rest of the chain is skipped.

q.q: What happens in C# if a case section in a switch statement has no break?
o: Execution falls through to the next case
q.why: C# forbids fall-through from a section containing statements; the compiler reports an error.

q.q: Which task suits a switch statement better than an else if chain?
o: Grading a mark into bands such as 50 to 74
Choosing an action from menu options 1 to 4
Checking that age is at least 18 and ID is shown
Checking a temperature is between 2 and 8
q.why: A switch matches one value against fixed constant options; ranges and combined conditions suit if statements.

q.q: Which condition correctly tests whether a fridge reading is outside the safe range 2 to 8 inclusive?
q.why: Outside means below 2 OR above 8. No value can be both, so && is never true; <= and >= wrongly include 2 and 8.

q.q: How many times does for (int k = 0; k <= 10; k += 2) run its body?
q.why: k takes 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10: six values.

q.q: Which loop outputs 5 4 3 2 1?
q.why: It starts at 5 and stops once i reaches 0; i >= 0 would also output 0, and i < 0 would never run.

q.q: When is the condition of a C# for loop tested?
q.why: It is a pre-test: if false initially, the body never runs. The update runs after every pass.

q.q: What is the last value output by for (int i = 2; i < 15; i += 3) Console.WriteLine(i);?
q.why: i takes 2, 5, 8, 11, 14; the next value, 17, fails i < 15.

q.q: Which loop is guaranteed to execute its body at least once?
q.why: In a post-condition loop the condition is only tested after the body has run.

q.q: A sentinel loop totals values until -1 is entered. The inputs are 8000, 6500, 9100, -1. What is the total?
q.why: The sentinel -1 is not data, so total = 8000 + 6500 + 9100 = 23 600.

q.q: A REPEAT … UNTIL score >= 50 loop is rewritten in C#. Which is correct?
q.why: UNTIL stops when its condition becomes true, so do…while must continue while it is false: the condition is reversed.

q.q: In a sentinel-controlled while loop, why is the next value read as the last statement of the body?
o: So that the loop is guaranteed to run at least once with any data
So that the sentinel value is added to the total before the loop ends
So that the program uses less memory while the loop is running
So that the condition tests each new value before it can be processed
q.why: Reading at the end means the sentinel is tested by the condition and never reaches the processing statements.

q.q: An outer loop runs 5 times and an inner loop runs 8 times on each pass. How many times does the inner body execute?
q.why: The inner loop runs completely for every pass of the outer loop: 5 × 8 = 40.

q.q: for (int row = 1; row <= 3; row++) contains for (int col = 1; col <= row; col++) which outputs one star each pass. How many stars are output altogether?
q.why: The inner limit depends on row: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 stars.

q.q: In the star program, the inner header is changed to for (int col = 1; col < row; col++). What is output on the third line?
q.why: With row = 3, col takes only 1 and 2, so two stars.

q.q: What is the main purpose of a trace table?
o: To record the values of variables as code is executed by hand
To store the program's data permanently between runs
To list each test's data and expected outcome
To design the layout of the user interface
q.why: A trace table tracks variable values statement by statement during a dry run. Listing data and expected outcomes is a test plan.

q.q: Which C# header is a procedure?
o: static int Total(int a, int b)
q.why: void means no value is returned, so it is a procedure.

q.q: Which statement best describes a function?
o: A subroutine that never takes any parameters
A subroutine that only displays output on screen
A prewritten subroutine supplied with the language
A subroutine that returns a single value to the calling code
q.why: Returning a value is the defining feature. Prewritten, tested subroutines are library routines.

q.q: Console.WriteLine, Math.Round and int.Parse are examples of...
q.why: Library routines are prewritten subroutines supplied with the language and already tested.

q.q: A function is declared static int Area(int w, int h). Which call is valid?
q.why: Two int arguments in the right order, with the result used. Arguments must match parameters in number, order and type.

q.q: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
o: An argument is named in the subroutine header; a parameter is the value supplied in the call
A parameter is named in the subroutine header; an argument is the value supplied in the call
A parameter is used only by functions; an argument is used only by procedures
A parameter is a global variable; an argument is a local variable in the subroutine
q.why: The parameter is in the definition; the argument is in the call.

q.q: MonthlyFee(int age, bool offPeak) sets fee to 20.00 if age < 18, otherwise 36.00, then multiplies by 0.75 if offPeak. What does MonthlyFee(42, true) return?
q.why: 42 is not under 18, so fee = 36.00; off-peak gives 36.00 × 0.75 = 27.00.

q.q: What happens to the statements after a return statement on the same path through a function?
o: They run after the value is returned
They run only if the value is zero
q.why: return sends the value back and ends the function immediately.

q.q: int n = 4; Triple(n); where Triple(int x) sets x = x * 3. What is n afterwards?
q.why: n is passed by value, so only the copy x is tripled; n is unchanged.

q.q: int score = 25; AddBonusByRef(ref score); where the parameter is ref int points and the method adds 10 to points. What is score afterwards?
q.why: By reference, the parameter refers to the original variable, so score itself becomes 35.

q.q: Which situation requires passing by reference?
o: A function that calculates the VAT due on a single price
A procedure that prints a customer's name on the screen
A function that checks whether a PIN has four digits
A procedure that swaps the values of two variables in the caller
q.why: The caller's variables must be changed, so references to them are needed.

q.q: What is a disadvantage of passing by reference?
o: The subroutine is not able to read the value that has been passed in
It always uses more memory than passing a copy of the value
It cannot be used with integer variables, only with strings
Unintended changes to the caller's variables can make errors hard to trace
q.why: Side effects leak back to the caller. Copying large data is the drawback of passing by value.

q.q: Where can a local variable declared inside a subroutine be accessed?
o: Anywhere in the program for the whole run
Only inside that subroutine or block
In any subroutine that is called afterwards
Only in the main program, not in subroutines
q.why: Its scope is limited to where it is declared.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of global variables?
o: Any subroutine can change them, so errors are hard to trace
They are destroyed at the end of each subroutine call
They must be passed as parameters to every subroutine
They are unable to store integer values
q.why: Unrestricted access makes unexpected changes hard to locate.

q.q: A subroutine is called three times. What happens to its local variable between calls?
o: It keeps its last value for the next call
It becomes a global variable after the first call
It is destroyed and created afresh on the next call
It is saved to a file until the next call
q.why: Locals exist only while their subroutine runs, so their value does not carry over.

q.q: LogVisit(int adults) declares local int bonusPoints = adults * 5 and adds it to the global-style field Club.totalPoints, which starts at 0. After LogVisit(3); LogVisit(4); what is Club.totalPoints?
q.why: The first call adds 3 × 5 = 15 and the second adds 4 × 5 = 20, giving 35. Each call creates a fresh bonusPoints.

q.q: Which is a genuine benefit of modular programming?
o: The finished program always runs faster than unmodular code
Syntax errors become impossible because each module is short
The program always uses less memory when it is running
Modules can be tested independently, making errors easier to locate
q.why: Independent testing is a key benefit. Modules do not make programs run faster.

q.q: Why must agreed interfaces be in place before a team builds modules in parallel?
o: So that global variables can be shared freely between all of the modules
So that no integration testing is needed once the modules are finished
So that modules written separately fit together correctly when integrated
So that the compiler can translate each module more quickly
q.why: Each programmer relies on agreed names, parameters and return types.

q.q: TicketCost(int n) multiplies n by £8.50 and applies a 10% discount if n >= 6. What does TicketCost(6) return?
q.why: 6 × £8.50 = £51.00; the 10% group discount gives £45.90.

q.q: Which describes a static data structure?
o: Its values cannot be changed once set
Its size is fixed when it is created
It is stored on secondary storage
It can hold different data types
q.why: Static refers to size, not values: the values in an array can change.

q.q: Which is the best structure for the names of shoppers joining a click-and-collect queue during the day?
q.why: The number of shoppers varies, so a dynamic list fits.

q.q: Why use a data structure rather than many separate variables such as mark1, mark2, … mark30?
o: Items share one identifier, so a loop can process them all
It always uses less memory than separate variables
It removes the need to choose a data type for the items
It makes the program compile more quickly
q.why: A single identifier with an index lets a loop handle every item.

q.q: For string[] towns = new string[6]; what is the index of the last element?
q.why: Indexes run from 0 to Length − 1.

q.q: For int[,] grid = new int[4, 7]; what does grid.GetLength(1) return?
q.why: Dimension 1 is the columns; GetLength(0) gives 4 rows and Length gives 28 elements.

q.q: Which loop header traverses every element of arr safely?
q.why: Start at 0 and stop before Length. <= Length throws IndexOutOfRangeException; starting at 1 misses the first element.

q.q: int[] litres = { 30, 0, 45, 25, 0, 50, 10 }; A loop finds the index of the largest value. What is it?
q.why: 50 is the largest value and it is at index 5 (counting from 0).

q.q: A list n holds 5, 8, 2. After n.RemoveAt(0); what is n[0]?
q.why: Removing index 0 shifts 8 to the front.

q.q: Which situation best suits a list rather than an array?
o: Customers joining a queue for a cash machine
q.why: The number of customers varies; the others are fixed sizes.

q.q: Which property gives the number of items in a C# List?
q.why: Lists use Count; arrays use Length. Mixing them up is a compile-time error.

q.q: A list rota holds Eimear, Jack, Sinead. After rota.Insert(1, "Tom"); rota.Remove("Jack"); what is rota.IndexOf("Sinead")?
q.why: Insert gives Eimear, Tom, Jack, Sinead; Remove gives Eimear, Tom, Sinead, so Sinead is at index 2.

q.q: What distinguishes a record from an array?
o: A record's fields can be of different data types
A record can only hold integer values
A record has no fixed set of fields
A record can only be stored on disk
q.why: Array elements share one type; record fields need not.

q.q: How is the price field of a record called item accessed in C#?
q.why: Fields are accessed with dot notation.

q.q: Why are records preferred to parallel arrays such as names[], numbers[] and heights[]?
o: Records use no memory until a field is accessed
Records are always faster to search than arrays
Records do not need to be declared before use
Related data stays together, so it cannot fall out of step
q.why: With parallel arrays, sorting or deleting in one and forgetting the others makes the data misaligned.

q.q: A program must add today's bookings to the end of bookings.txt without losing earlier ones. Which mode should it use?
q.why: Append keeps existing data and adds to the end; write overwrites the file completely.

q.q: What does "Ross,42,7.5".Split(',') return?
q.why: Split always returns a string array; converting each field is a separate step.

q.q: Why must a file be closed after writing?
o: So that the file is converted to CSV format
So buffered data is written to disk and the file is released
So that the file is made read-only for others
So that the file is deleted from memory and disk
q.why: Closing (or a using block) flushes the buffer and frees the file for other programs.

q.q: A program reads the line "Fionn,17,false" and splits it into f. Which statement correctly gets the age as a number?
q.why: Everything read from a text file is text, so the second field (index 1) must be converted with int.Parse.

q.q: Why is data in a List lost when the program closes?
o: It is held in RAM, which is released when the program ends
Lists are automatically deleted every hour
Lists can only hold strings, which are temporary
The compiler removes it when the program ends
q.why: Program memory in RAM does not persist; files on secondary storage do.

q.q: Which C# method checks whether a file is present before reading it?
q.why: File.Exists returns true or false.

q.q: Why is checking File.Exists not enough on its own to avoid file errors?
o: File.Exists only works for files that have already been opened
File.Exists deletes the file if it is open in another program
File.Exists can only check files stored in the cloud, not on disk
The file could be deleted or locked between the check and the read
q.why: That is why exception handling is still needed.

q.q: Which statement about validation is true?
o: It checks data is reasonable and obeys rules
It guarantees that the data is correct
It is always carried out by a person
It checks the data matches the source
q.why: Validation checks data is allowable, not that it is correct. Matching the source is verification.

q.q: A user is asked to type a new password twice. What is this?
q.why: The two entries are compared to confirm accuracy.

q.q: Which check would reject 'BT7A 1NN' as a Northern Ireland postcode?
q.why: It does not match the expected pattern (BT followed by a digit, then a valid layout).

q.q: Why use int.TryParse rather than int.Parse when validating input?
o: It also performs a range check on the converted number
It accepts decimal values and rounds them to whole numbers
It runs faster because it skips the type conversion
It returns false instead of throwing an exception for invalid text
q.why: TryParse lets the program re-prompt without crashing.

q.q: When does a finally block run?
o: Whether or not an exception occurs
q.why: finally always runs, making it ideal for tidying up such as closing a file.

q.q: Which exception is thrown by int.Parse("12.5")?
q.why: "12.5" is not a valid integer string. OverflowException is for numbers too large for an int.

q.q: Why must catch (Exception) come after catch (FormatException)?
o: C# runs the catch blocks in reverse order, starting from the last one
The general type would catch everything first, so the specific handler would never run
The general Exception handler is slower, so it should be checked last
FormatException is not a type of Exception, so it needs its own block
q.why: The first matching catch runs, so specific handlers must precede general ones (the compiler rejects the wrong order).

q.q: scores = { 12, 18, 9 }. A try block reads r = 1 and players = 0, then outputs scores[r] / players. There are catches for FormatException, IndexOutOfRangeException and DivideByZeroException, and a finally block. What happens?
o: The DivideByZeroException message only, as finally is skipped
The program crashes, because 18 / 0 cannot be caught
q.why: 18 / 0 is integer division by zero, so that catch runs; finally always runs afterwards.

q.q: A program compiles and runs but always outputs one less than the correct count. What type of error is this?
q.why: It runs without crashing but gives the wrong result.

q.q: Which error is reported by the compiler and stops the program being built?
q.why: A missing semicolon is a syntax error, which prevents compilation.

q.q: Accessing names[5] in a 5-element array is which type of error?
q.why: It compiles, then throws IndexOutOfRangeException while running.

q.q: int age = "sixteen"; is grammatically correct C# but has no valid meaning. Which type of error is it?
q.why: Semantic errors are grammatical but meaningless; C# catches many, like this type mismatch, at compile time.

q.q: A field accepts 1 to 50. Which pair are both extreme (boundary) data?
q.why: Extreme data is exactly on the limits and should be accepted; 0 and 51 are invalid.

q.q: What type of test data is "twelve" for a field that expects a whole number?
q.why: It is the wrong type, so it should be rejected.

q.q: After fixing a failed test, what should the programmer do?
q.why: The fix might introduce new errors elsewhere (regression testing).

q.q: Which tool runs a called subroutine as a single step without entering it?
q.why: Step over executes the whole call at once; step into enters it.

q.q: An exception is thrown inside a subroutine called from three places. Which tool shows which caller was involved?
q.why: The call stack lists the chain of calls that led to the current line.

q.q: What is the main purpose of a breakpoint?
o: To pause execution at a chosen line so its state can be examined
To run the program one line at a time from the start
To show the chain of calls that led to the current line
To stop the program compiling until an error is fixed
q.why: A breakpoint pauses so values can be inspected. Running line by line is stepping.

q.q: Which error can no translator detect?
q.why: Logic errors are legal code that does the wrong thing.

q.q: An interpreted program updates 50 records then hits a syntax error in line 80. What is the risk?
o: None, because the interpreter undoes the changes
The error is reported before line 1 runs
The records are rolled back automatically
The data may be left half-updated
q.why: Earlier statements have already executed when the interpreter reaches the faulty line.

q.q: Why are run-time errors possible even in a program that compiles without errors?
o: Compilers check only the comments, not the statements in the code
They depend on data supplied while running, which the compiler cannot know
Run-time errors are syntax errors the compiler chose to ignore
Compilers cannot translate any division or array statements
q.why: For example, a divisor of zero only arises from particular input.
